title: 3 Months into Using AI for Game Assets and Here Is My Honest Cost Breakdown
author: Ok_Reference_1100
selftext:
olo dev, making a roguelike. Budget is basically my savings. Been using AI 3D generation for 3 months and wanted to share actual numbers since everyone talks about this stuff in vague terms.

Subscription cost: \~$15/month = $45 total so far. I tried a few tools and settled on one that had the best hit rate for my use case (Meshy if anyone's curious).

Assets generated: roughly 180 total attempts.  
Assets actually used in game: 94.  
Hit rate: about 52%.

The other 48% were either unusable (bad geometry, wrong style) or duplicates where I generated multiple versions and picked the best one.

Cleanup time per asset: ranges from 5 minutes (simple props) to 45 minutes (characters that need retopo). Average maybe 15 minutes in Blender.

If I value my time at $0 (lol solo dev life) the cost per usable asset is about $0.48. If I value cleanup time at even $20/hour, it's more like $5.50 per asset including my labor.

Compare that to: asset store packs ($2-5 per asset but they don't match your style) or modeling it myself (2-6 hours per asset at my skill level).

The real savings aren't just money though. It's momentum. When I need a new prop I can have something in-engine in 30 minutes instead of putting it on a todo list that never gets done.

What AI generation is bad at: characters with specific designs, anything mechanical with moving parts, weapons (always too thin), and maintaining consistent art style across many assets.

What it's great at: environment props, organic shapes, rocks/vegetation, and anything where "close enough" is good enough.

Would I recommend it to other solo devs? Yeah but go in with realistic expectations. It's not free art. It's faster art that still needs work.

replies.author: Nez_Coupe
replies.body: I’m with you. And with OP, it’s a momentum builder. I’ve only been doing game dev (I’m a data manager/SWE by trade) for a few months, and asset generation was extremely slow at first. Like, I don’t think I have that kind of time to hash out and develop my ideas fully. I do a lot of pixel art, and for statics + animation for every player character and npc, it’s simply too much for be to do everything. My new workflow is basically midjourney (I describe my nitty gritty details and feel) —> manually create a static front view sprite -> feed to GPT-image gen 2 with a template sprite sheet -> basic sprite done -> manually edit 3-4 hours to fix any misses. I just started this last week, and I can get a character basically fully done is 5-6 hours tops, versus what seems like a month for my first player character doing it all manually.

comments.author: Gold_Citron5264
comments.body:
I'm currently using meshyAI to generate character models for a feature film. (it's a new film releasing in a few months. Can't say which rn due to nda)
It's a bit of an edge case as the sequence we're doing is a 2 minute animated sequence in a live action film and no-one was really anal like they are in animation. We used gemini to make character sheets and turnarounds then generated the models. We generated them in a few passes. First the whole body, then used gemini to make close-ups of the face and did those on a separate pass. We also generated the heads without any hair as we did the hair in blender with curves (anime stylized vibes). MeshyAI has a quad remesh feature which was kinda useful for the bodies. We had to manually retopo the heads for optimal deformations as we required facial animation. All in all, we created 7 characters (plus nude versions so 14 in total), and had them all rigged and animation ready within 2 weeks. That's unheard of before this Ai boom. The models had many issues which we had to patch up during production. Would've been all cleaned up had we had an extra week or two in pre-prod but without meshy we wouldn't have made that deadline at all. We were also able to create weapons. A big hammer, dagger and a katana/Dao style weapons. They all came out decent and on the first try. I think we maybe used 1/4 of our tokens for the month too.

comments.author: xthingsdone
comments.body:
That 52% hit rate actually sounds pretty solid.  
  
The momentum point is probably the biggest advantage. Cost per asset matters, but not getting stuck for hours on something non-critical is what really keeps a project moving.  
  
The consistency issue is real too. Individual assets can look fine, but once you place them together, the style mismatch starts to show unless you spend extra time fixing it.  
  
How are you dealing with that over time? Are you standardizing prompts and references, or just accepting a bit of inconsistency to keep things moving?

comments.author: Delicious-Shower8401
comments.body:
biggest problem with meshy was paying for too many bad or unusable generations. sometimes the result had bad geometry, wrong style, or just was not worth cleaning up, but the credits were already gone.

the solution for me was switching to hyper3d / rodin. you can generate and retry without spending credits if the result is bad, and only pay when you actually like the result enough to download or use it. that makes the whole workflow way more user friendly, especially when you need a lot of iterations.

also, rodin gen-2.5 feels much stronger for my current workflow. cleaner mesh output, better low poly results, nicer uvs, and less cleanup in blender / ue5. meshy feels heavily advertised right now, but the results honestly have been pretty weak for me lately.
